title: Appraisal Gaps: What Happens When the Home Appraises Low
description: When an appraisal comes in below the contract price, buyers and agents have options. Here's how appraisal gaps work and the strategies that keep deals together.
image_alt: A small model house next to a magnifying glass

faq.a: It's the difference between the contract price and the appraised value when the appraisal comes in lower than the price.

faq.q: Can a low appraisal be challenged?
faq.a: Yes. A reconsideration of value can be requested through the lender if there are factual errors or better comparable sales the appraiser didn't consider.

faq.q: Does a low appraisal change the loan amount?
faq.a: Lenders base the loan on the lower of price or appraised value, so a low appraisal can increase the cash the buyer needs to keep the same loan terms.

body_html:
Few moments in escrow cause more stress than a low appraisal. The buyer worries about losing the house, the seller worries about losing the price, and both agents start fielding calls. The good news is that a low appraisal is a problem with a defined set of solutions.

Why the gap matters

Lenders base the loan on the lower of the purchase price or the appraised value. If a home under contract appraises below the price, the loan amount the buyer planned for may not support the deal as written. Someone has to bridge the difference, or the terms need to change.

The five ways deals get back on track

OptionHow it worksBest when
Reconsideration of valueSubmit better comps or correct factual errors through the lenderThe appraiser missed relevant sales or features
Seller reduces the pricePrice drops to or toward appraised valueMarket data supports the appraisal
Buyer covers the gapBuyer brings additional cashBuyer has reserves and wants the home
Split the differencePrice moves partway; buyer covers the restBoth sides want to keep the deal
Restructure the loanDifferent down payment or loan typeThe buyer has flexibility in financing

Making a reconsideration of value work

A reconsideration is most effective when it's factual and specific. Emotional appeals don't move appraisers. What helps:

  • Closed sales the appraiser didn't use that are truly comparable in size, condition, and location
  • Corrections to factual errors like square footage, bedroom count, or upgrades
  • Clear, organized presentation through the lender, which manages communication with the appraiser

Pending sales and active listings can provide context, but closed sales carry the most weight.

Appraisal gap language in offers

In competitive markets, some buyers include language committing to cover part or all of a potential gap. It can strengthen an offer, but only if the buyer truly has the cash. Before writing it in, confirm with the loan officer how much the buyer can cover without hurting reserves or loan eligibility. Pair it with an understanding of the financing contingency so the client knows what's protected and what isn't.

Preventing surprises

  1. Price-check aggressive offers against recent closed sales before writing
  2. Provide the appraiser with a list of upgrades and relevant comps at the inspection, through the proper channels
  3. Make sure the property is accessible and presentable on appraisal day
  4. Build a contingency timeline that leaves room for a reconsideration if needed

What a low appraisal means for each side

It helps to understand how the gap looks from each seat at the table, because that shapes what each party is willing to do.

For the buyer, the immediate question is cash. If the loan is based on the appraised value, keeping the same price usually means a larger down payment. Buyers who planned to keep a healthy cushion after closing need to decide how much of that cushion they're willing to use. Lenders may also look at reserves after the change, so the buyer's loan officer should rerun the numbers before anyone commits.

For the seller, the question is whether the next buyer would face the same appraisal. If the home goes back on the market, the new buyer's lender will likely order its own appraisal, and the value may land in a similar place. A seller who understands that is often more willing to meet in the middle.

For both agents, the clock matters. Contingency deadlines keep running while everyone negotiates, so it's worth agreeing quickly on whether to request a reconsideration and whether to extend any timelines in writing.

Cash buyers and low appraisals

Buyers paying cash don't need an appraisal for a lender, but many still order one to protect themselves. A low value doesn't block the purchase in that case, but it's useful information for negotiation. If your buyer plans to finance later with a cash-out refinance or a delayed financing option, the future appraisal matters for that loan too.

  • Ask whether the contract includes an appraisal contingency even for cash, if the buyer wants that protection
  • Make sure the buyer understands that future borrowing will be based on future appraisals, not today's price
  • Keep comps and upgrade lists on file in case they're needed later

The takeaway

A low appraisal isn't the end of a deal. It's a negotiation with clear options. Agents who prepare buyers in advance, document their comps, and coordinate with the loan officer quickly usually find a path that works for both sides.
